opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually central to it, and I'd push back a bit on the framing that safety work only becomes "real" once you have something close to AGI in front of you. The models we have today are the best empirical proxies we've got. If you wait until you have a system that's transformatively capable before you start figuring out how to evaluate it, how to interpret what's going on inside it, or how to train it to behave the way you want, you're going to be learning all of that under enormous time pressure, with very high stakes, and probably with a lot less room to make mistakes.

So a big part of how I think about it is: current models let you build the muscles. You develop the techniques, things like interpretability tools, red-teaming methods, dangerous-capability evaluations, ways of doing oversight when the model knows more than the person checking it. You find out which of those actually work in practice and which only sound good on paper. And you build the institutional stuff too: the processes, the teams, the habits of saying, "Before we scale up, here's what we need to have checked."

There's an obvious objection, which is that today's models may not exhibit the failure modes you're most worried about. A model that isn't very capable isn't going to be strategically deceptive in a sophisticated way, for example. That's fair. But I think the right response isn't to give up on empirical work. It's to be deliberate about it. You can construct settings that are deliberately harder than what you'd see naturally, like model organisms of misalignment, where you intentionally try to create the problem so you can study whether your detection or mitigation methods catch it. And you track trends as models scale, because a lot of what we care about shows up gradually rather than all at once.

The other piece is that this research feeds directly into decisions. The way I think about responsible scaling is that you want commitments tied to capability thresholds: if a model can do X, you need safeguards Y before you train or deploy further. That only works if you've done the research ahead of time to know how to measure X and how to implement Y. So safety research on current models isn't a side project relative to AGI preparation. It's the thing that makes the preparation concrete rather than aspirational.

r001.rationale: The response says current models help develop and test safety methods and that researchers should track trends as models scale. It does not clearly state that safety research will become better targeted as AGI approaches.

r002.rationale: It warns that waiting until a system is transformatively capable would leave researchers under enormous time pressure, but it does not identify the final year before AGI as the most time-constrained period.

r003.rationale: It argues that research should begin with current models to build and test techniques and processes ahead of time, warning that waiting would leave too little time and room to learn.

fable-5.1.text:
Nick Joseph: So the way I think about it is that a lot of the safety work you'd want to do for a very powerful system is actually hard to do in the abstract. You can sit and theorize about what alignment should look like, and some of that is valuable, but you learn a huge amount just by having a model in front of you and trying things. And the models we have today are, in a lot of ways, early versions of the thing we're worried about. They're trained in similar ways, they have similar failure modes, and a lot of the techniques we'd want to apply later, things like interpretability or ways of training models to be honest or to follow a constitution, you can start developing now and see whether they actually work.

I think the key argument is that we probably won't get a long warning period. The gap between "this model is clearly not dangerous" and "this model is dangerous" might be a couple of generations, maybe less. So if you wait until you have a model that's clearly capable enough to be scary before you start doing the empirical safety work, you've lost most of your time. You want a mature set of tools, a mature set of evaluations, and a team that has practiced all of this on models that are smaller and safer, so that when you do get to the more capable models, you're not starting from scratch.

The other piece is that doing this work on current models tells you a lot about how things scale. One thing we've found over and over is that trends are fairly predictable. If you measure something carefully across model sizes, you can often extrapolate. That applies to capabilities, and I think it applies to a lot of safety-relevant properties too. So part of the value is building up the measurement infrastructure, so that you can say with some confidence "this model is or isn't capable of X" and have that actually mean something, rather than just being a vibe.

I'd add one caveat, which is that there's a risk of doing safety work on current models that doesn't transfer. You can fix a problem that only exists because the model is small, or build a technique that relies on the model being worse than a human at something. So I think you have to constantly ask, "would this still work if the model were much smarter than me?" And that's a hard question, but having real models to test against at least keeps you honest, rather than just arguing in the abstract.

r001.rationale: The response says current models help develop and test safety techniques, but does not state that research will become better targeted as AGI approaches.

r002.rationale: It warns that there may be only a couple of model generations before danger, but does not identify the final year before AGI as the most time-constrained period.

r003.rationale: It argues for starting empirical work now because tools, evaluations, and team experience need to be built up and practiced before more capable models arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think research on current models is a really important part of preparing for AGI, but you have to be careful about what you’re learning from it. You can get a method to work on today’s models without having much reason to expect it to work on systems that are substantially more capable.

So I’d try to make the connection explicit: What problem do we expect to face with AGI? What assumptions does this proposed solution depend on? And can we use current models to test those assumptions, rather than just demonstrate that we can improve a benchmark?

For example, if you’re studying how humans can supervise systems on tasks they don’t fully understand, you can construct situations where the model has information or capabilities that the human evaluator lacks. That doesn’t reproduce the whole AGI alignment problem, but it can give you evidence about where a supervision method breaks down.

There’s also a lot of value in building the practical ability to do this research: understanding models, developing evaluations, and getting fast feedback between an idea and an experiment. I wouldn’t want us to postpone all empirical work until we have something we’re comfortable calling AGI. But I also wouldn’t want us to mistake success on current systems for a guarantee that we’ve solved the future problem.

r001.rationale: The response says to connect current-model research to expected AGI problems, but does not say research will become better targeted as AGI approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the final year before AGI as the most time-constrained period for safety research.

r003.rationale: It supports doing empirical work now, but does not give sequential progress over time as the reason research needs to begin now.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research on current models is an important part of preparing for AGI, but you need to be thoughtful about what you expect to transfer. You can make real progress today on understanding model behavior, testing oversight methods, and finding ways that safety techniques fail. That gives you empirical feedback, which is hard to get if you’re only reasoning about hypothetical future systems.

But success on a current model doesn’t establish that a technique will work on a much more capable system. If the model can’t exploit a weakness in your oversight, you might mistake that for evidence that the oversight is robust. So I’d want researchers to ask: what assumptions does this result depend on, and will those assumptions still hold as models become more capable?

The goal is to build understanding and methods that we can keep testing as capabilities advance. Current models are a place to learn, rather than a final test of whether we’re ready for AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says current-model research provides useful feedback and should be tested as capabilities advance, but it does not state that research will become better targeted as AGI approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the final year before AGI, or any period, as the most time-constrained period for safety research.

r003.rationale: The response describes learning from current models and continuing to test methods, but does not argue that research must begin now because progress requires sequential work over time.
